speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance on a day when the figures indicate that for the first five months of 1978 the rate of inflation in this country was higher than before the controls program was brought in. The minister knows that when this government imposed controls, against its promise, it forecast a 4 per cent inflation rate for the fall of this year. When the minister brought in his budget, he forecast a 7 per cent inflation rate for 1978. Today's figures show that following the present trend in this country we will have an inflation rate of at least 11 per cent.
Will the Minister of Finance tell us what, in his analysis, has gone wrong? Why has the government failed to deal with inflation as they promised they could, what changes does he intend to introduce, and when will the House of Commons receive those changes?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 was disappointed to see the inflation rate was high this morning. It was mainly due to food prices, which have increased very substantially mainly due to the beef cycle. We are out of controls-

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF VEGETABLES
speechtext:
My final supplementary question is to the Prime Minister, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture. I am sure the right hon. gentleman has noticed that the price of vegetables has gone up by some 39 per cent in the last year. He knows we are not self-sufficient in the production of vegetables, beef, chicken and hogs; indeed, in almost all the foods in respect of which prices have risen so sharply.
I would ask the Prime Minister what he intends to do to make this country more self-sufficient in the production of food. If you exclude grain and oilseeds, last year, according to the government's own figures, we were a net importer of food to the tune of $1.8 billion. What does the right hon. gentleman intend to do to ensure that we produce more food, which would give a better income to farmers, a stable price to consumers and more jobs to Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF VEGETABLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand this question was dealt with in part before my arrival in the House. I can only repeat what has already been said, that the hon. member is right, we are not self-sufficient in food, and that some 30 per cent of what we consume is imported, a circumstance which is in large part due to the seasonal nature of our production. We import food because in many instances we cannot grow it in Canada during the season when it is required for consumption here.
In the case of beef, the single factor most responsible for the increase in the food price index, the beef cycle as predicted has caught up with us and we are now paying a high price because for the last two years beef producers have been receiving a very low price. Now that they are getting a higher price-a more reasonable one-we are sympathetic to the consumer, but we cannot blame the beef producer or attempt to take it out on him.

speechtext:
Hon. members will be aware that the matter of support staff positions for all members of the House of Commons have been under consideration for some time. I will be tabling a document today in that regard.
Before going on to routine proceedings, I thought that all hon. members would want to be informed of some rather important and significant steps that have been taken with respect to the staff of members' offices, particularly described as support staff for members of the House of Commons. In light of comments that have been made somehow a number of negotiations and efforts that have been taking place over the last 12 months regarding the support staff of members have managed to be either overlooked or ignored in discussions that have taken place with respect to the positions of staff of the House of Commons.
I should like to report to the House that the study is an excellent piece of work which has been done in the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services in respect particularly to the staff of members of the House of Commons. I say that in this way because, with respect to the provisions which we have recently enacted in regard to salaries of personnel of the House of Commons, we have always endeavoured to establish a balance which would seem to be just and reasonable between those who work for the House of Commons and the taxpayers who pay all of the bills for the operation of the House of Commons by trying to find out whether or not all of the members of the personnel of the House of Commons have been paid in such a way as to reflect favourably on their counterparts in the public service and in the private sector. By endeavouring to negotiate increases annually which keep employees of the House of Commons slightly ahead of their counterparts in the public service and the private sector, we feel certain that, without collective bargaining, they are enjoying the benefits of the best of both worlds.
In respect, however, to support staff for members of the House of Commons, who constitute a substantial aspect of the personnel of the House of Commons, it has long been recognized that this effort to tie support staff positions in the offices of the members of the House of Commons to some equivalent positions in the public service has not been a satisfactory arrangement because, obviously, many members have personnel and support staff who fulfil functions which cannot be described in the public service. By attempting to correlate those positions to positions in the public service, we have met with the rather legitimate concern on behalf of the support staff of the members of the House of Commons that, while the salary ranges may reflect favourably in respect to the secretarial positions in the public service, their responsibilities do not correlate accurately. Therefore, the objective of the very excellent and thorough work in the standing committee has been to find a regime which would liberate the support staff from this correlation to positions in the public service which are primarily secretarial in nature.

June 14, 1978
Oral Questions
The Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services has done a very excellent review of this situation, and after careful consideration and several studies they came forward with recommendations which were recently reviewed by the commissioners of internal economy. As I say, the object was to establish a new and special classification for the support staff for members of the House of Commons. After the commissioners of internal economy reviewed the recommendations, it was agreed that effective at the beginning of the next parliament they would become operative.
Since this parliament is now continuing for some time, it was recently asked by the members' services committee whether that implementation date could be fixed in a different way, and the commissioners of internal economy reviewed the matter and agreed that it would be appropriate to make the recommendations effective September 1 of this year. Accordingly, I am now able to table a schedule on classifications of support staff for members which we feel reflects the unique responsibilities of persons who work in the offices of the members of the House of Commons as support staff, and gives an option of several different formulae that may be adopted by a member of the House, depending on the particular needs that he or she may have. This is all within a fixed budget that is attributable to the support staff for the member.
I table this schedule today simply to indicate that the matter has been under review for almost a year and has been the subject of very careful and very extensive study. I would also say that between now and the implementation date members will find, upon tabling of this minute of the commissioners of internal economy, that they will now enjoy a number of options in terms of employment as of September 1 and positions and salary ranges which are freed from any correlation in the public service.
In addition to that, by the implementation date of September 1 it is hoped that a further option may be arrived at in co-operation with the management and members' services committee and the commissioners of internal economy, both of whom have expressed agreement in principle with this further option, and that is an option which may release some of the constraints that are upon the constituency offices in terms of the over-all staff requirements for members. That is to say simply that a further option will be studied to see whether or not one of the senior positions in the scheme which I am now tabling may be utilized in the constituency office. That, of course, bears with it a number of other consequences in terms of salary and other allowances in the constituency office, and it is worthy of very careful exploration and more precise definition. I merely wanted to indicate to members of the House that that matter will be further studied in the hope that that option can also be achieved in time for the implementation date of September 1.

subsubtopic: MR. DINSDALE-DELAY IN TABLING POST OFFICE ANNUAL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) on Thursday, June 8, 1978. I should like to indicate that I was absent from the House when it was raised. Whenever I am absent from the House, it is always for very good reasons. An international philatelic exhibition was being held in Toronto, and I had to be there to welcome the general director of the Universal Postal Union and the new postmaster general of the United States. I can say, therefore, that I had excellent reasons not to be present in the House, because I was fulfilling the duties of my office.
The question of privilege which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris raised had several parts, the first one dealing with his appearance before the Standing Committee on Transport. Mr. Speaker, I am not the one who decides what the procedures of a committee are going to be. It is the chairman of the committee who decides and who must defend his position. I do not believe that there is a question of privilege in this case.
In second place, I will deal with the tabling of the annual report of the Post Office. It was quite normal, as I was appointed Postmaster General at the beginning of February and knew that the annual report should have been tabled at that time, that I should, as minister responsible for the Post Office, look at what was written in this report before tabling it; the report was tabled in both official languages within 14 weeks. After checking the records at the National Library and according to my information, I must say that since 1956, the Post Office annual report has never been tabled on time. I do not believe that I can be accused of starting a new trend. The 1977-78 report will be tabled on time.
A third point mentioned in the question of privilege is that during a meeting of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, the hon. member obtained from myself and my officials four copies of the annual report, two in French and two in English. He complains that he was left with the two reports in French and that these were of no use to him since he does not understand this language. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry about this, but one of his colleagues, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who was next to him, laid hands on both English copies. That is why the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was left with both French copies.
I should also like to note, Mr. Speaker, that in 1956-57, as several members on the other side will recall, the English version of the Post Office report was tabled on October 18, 1957, and the French version on June 22, eight months later. I believe that we were right to hand the report in both official languages to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. I am very sorry that he cannot read French, but he still had the report.
Order Paper Questions
Mr. Speaker, the fourth point mentioned in his question of privilege concerned the Crown corporation. I suggest that he read the minutes of the committee on transport on this subject. A committee made up of representatives of three departments is looking into this matter and the report will be made public in due time.
The fifth and last point concerns the postal rates increases and the allegation that the government illegally increased those rates. Mr. Speaker, I believe that even if we feel that the method used to increase the rates was quite legal, the matter is now sub judice and it is wiser to leave the decision to the judges. So, Mr. Speaker, I think that in the five points I have made, I do not see any grounds for a question of privilege, but obviously the decision is in the hands of the Chair.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: That, in the opinion of this House, the present government is the most wasteful in Canadian history and has established an unmatchable standard of incompetence, leading to today's high inflation and record high unemployment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: Hon. members will note that, in accordance with subsection (11) of Standing Order 58, proceedings on this motion will expire later this day at the ordinary hour of adjournment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that in this motion today there is a warning that all of us here at the seat of the federal government in Ottawa should heed. I sincerely believe that the present form of parliamentary democracy in Canada will become unstuck and will fail in the next decade if we do not return this federal system of government to a standard of accountability and morality acceptable to the Canadian people.
Anyone engaged in productive work, being accountable at all times to the tax collector, has to be not only outraged but actually frightened at the standard of incompetence and indifference with which this government manages our tax resources. We are now at the point where, for every dollar we earn, we collect only 80 cents. A person lucky enough to have a job must work from nine o'clock in the morning until two o'clock in the afternoon to pay his tax. Only after two o'clock in the afternoon is he working for his own spending money.
We are at the point where the rules of the game in the private sector are now so uncertain and confused that there is little incentive to expand and to risk savings which on an after tax basis are too expensive to risk. We are at the point where entrepreneurial talent and capital, aware of what has happened in England and seeing that the "English disease" is now well upon us in Canada, have left the country for a form of government which nurtures that aspect of man that reacts to incentives.
At the root of one of the problems this government faces is the disastrous situation within the federal system where mandarin status is measured by man-years and by the size of budget and expenditure control. Nowhere today does one find that old fashioned concern for the taxpayers' dollar. Nowhere within the system can one find a top level concern for what the tax resource is spent on for the value received in return for an expenditure of our tax resource.
Our work in the committees of this House allows us to meet some very bright and able people in our public service. Coming from the street, as I do, and from the world of productive work-and by that I mean adding to the value of goods in a competitive marketplace-what I see as a very basic problem is a legislation drafting environment, a resource allocation and

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
management process that has absolutely isolated itself from the world of productive work and the value system of the taxpayer.
To people like myself, Ottawa is an "Alice in Wonderland", a fairyland where accountability in terms fundamental to a taxpayer is completely lacking. When 1 say that the present government is the most wasteful in Canadian history with a standard of incompetence, and yes, morality that threatens the very concept of peace, order and good government, I owe the House some examples to back up that statement.
Some years ago when the late Arthur Laing, a former minister of public works, retired he made a statement in Vancouver to the effect that, if the Canadian people really knew what was going on, there would be a revolt. Although never a supporter of Arthur Laing, I knew the man well and his statement troubled me. Therefore, when elected in 1974 I started to look around the Department of Public Works to see what his remark was all about.
In the late 1960s, I guess about the year 1968, a successful history of Crown construction with a system of checks and balances and accountability came to an end. We saw the evolution of politically well-connected developers moving in on the domain of the Department of Public Works to the point where, in the next decade, that department was reduced to little more than a real estate management function with the National Capital Commission acting as its agent in the capital region.
For example, in the 1960s there were three major building projects being undertaken by the Department of Public Works. One was the Department of External Affairs building which was a $69 million project. There was a building to house the Ministry of Transport, a $68 million project. They were planning and had even expropriated land in LeBreton flats for a $100 million building to house the Department of National Defence.
The story, as l understand it, goes something like this. The external affairs building, as we know it today in all its beauty on Sussex Drive, was completed. The building designed for the Ministry of Transport was completed, but into it was moved the Department of National Defence. The Place de Ville tower, moving up through all height restrictions in place in the city of Ottawa to protect the aesthetic features of the Peace Tower, was built to house the Department of Transport.
That left us with LeBreton flats, 122 acres, which has cost the people of Canada a little over $53 million; in other words $434,426 per acre. Remember that this land was expropriated from 258 owners for a national building in 1962. When we now see property of this cost being used for another purpose, such as subsidized public housing, we really have to wonder where all our marbles have gone. How can the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) expect us to believe that the story that the eight public housing units built on one quarter of an acre of this land at a stated cost of $40,000 to $46,000 is true when the land value per unit is over $13,000? If Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation claims that the land cost is only $25,000 for the one quarter acre on which

these eight units are built, who is going to pay for the difference of $83,000 for that one quarter acre which has a real book value of $108,600? Where in public accounts will this difference show up? What department of government will subsidize this difference? The Minister of State for Urban Affairs is talking about 425 public housing units at 30 units per acre on land that has a value and a direct cost of over $434,000 per acre. That land ends up costing $15,000 per subsidized public housing unit.
Another example to explain the rationale behind this motion is the CN recapitalization bill which we have finished debating in committee and in this House. We allowed CN a debt cancellation and capitalization program so that they can go into the private money markets, which are very disciplined, for more of their borrowing to meet those needs. This is the third recapitalization in which the Crown corporation has been involved, and some of us are very concerned lest the same thing happen as happened after the 1952 recapitalization when the CNR went on a spending spree and spent $1.8 billion.
In talking about waste and incompetence let me draw attention to the ferry crossing which the CNR has been asked to provide between Matane, Baie Comeau and Quebec city. Originally Canadian Pacific had carried out a feasibility study on the Baie Comeau-Quebec city project. They found that with a $10 million capital investment they could provide a completely workable service which could earn them a profit upon which they would have the privilege of paying taxes to both the provincial and the federal governments.
Then the politicians got into the act. They asked for a triangular run between Matane, Baie Comeau and Quebec city. Further feasibility studies were carried out and the CPR concluded that the project was not feasible. So the CNR entered the scene. Mr. Speaker, the CNR is in for $100 million and feasibility studies show there is no way in which the company can ever turn a profit. This is the kind of waste and decisionmaking which illustrate the need for a system which will give the people some voice in the decisionmaking process followed by these corporations.
I turn now to the operations of the National Capital Commission in Hull, Quebec. They have led to empty office towers in Ottawa, to space left unoccupied to the financial detriment of the whole community. This is waste without equal in the peacetime history of Canada. Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project, the nature of which insults every working taxpayer in Canada, has yet to be explained in believable terms by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan).
Some non. Members: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
But over and above this new assault on the public purse, we now learn that the National Capital Commission and the government have spent $150 million on roads in the city of Hull. Where else in Canada, including Ottawa, has such a level of federal assistance been given to any town or city? Why cannot the productivity of the port of Vancouver be
June 14, 1978

increased immeasurably by the use of $150 million in grants from the federal government to create the multi-level crossings which are needed to serve this port, a port which is in an obsolete condition? This amount of money would enable the port to be restored to a high state of productivity and reduce the amount of energy and time lost in coping with single level crossings such as are presently in place.
For a further example of the waste that concerns me I turn to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It is a small matter, some might say, but we uncovered an appropriation for a million dollars to enable the Indian arts and crafts fund to begin to buy and put together a collection of Indian art and offer some work and social services to the Indian bands. It is bad enough that the department should go $400,000 beyond the appropriation. It is serious enough that no discipline should have been exercised other than moving to another job the officer who was responsible so that he could not continue to overspend appropriations which had been voted. But when I find that money voted for a social service within the Indian communities has been used to purchase $44,000 worth of stamped out metal from a works in Vancouver, and that most of it has ended up as junk which cannot be sold, I am incensed.
How can any of us believe that the expenditure of this $44,000 ever benefited any Indian band or any Indian artist? Who has enough influence with the government to obtain a $44,000 order for stamped out Indian artifacts which are not even genuine? This is the kind of waste and incompetence which sets up a fury in my mind and which I want to stop before I cease to be a member of parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
I could give many further examples but I will use the example of the Ehettasaht Co-op. The Department of Indian Affairs rushed in and in a period of eight months went through some $5.5 million, leaving behind an unbelievable tale of waste and woe in the private sector. And then the organization went bankrupt. Where is the planning, the heart, the sensitivity to the use of public funds when it comes to examples like this? There were two or three similar cases in Alberta.
This is the type of misuse of the tax resource which will cause the system to become unstuck. We cannot allow it to continue at its present level. Within the Department of Indian Affairs we have seen rip-off after rip-off, innocent disaster after innocent disaster. In trying to give Indian bands independence, allowing them to spend sums of money more or less unsupervised, the department has left them without any training or ability to account for the funds granted to them. We are not doing these bands a favour by leaving them alone in this situation, part of the spill-over of carelessness in utilizing tax revenue.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation troubles me. Section 3 of the Broadcasting Act reads as follows:
Government Waste
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be owned and controlled by Canadians to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political and social fabric of Canada.
In the last decade this Crown corporation has cost us more than $2.5 billion. In this past year of restraint the number of employees increased from 11,293 to 12,222, and spending increased by $55 million compared with the previous year. When one recalls the words of section 3 of the Broadcasting Act, can one honestly say that the corporation is fulfilling the purposes for which it was brought into being?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: No!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
I cannot. I think the corporation has failed and that somehow or other we must strengthen the act so as to bring it under control, or else sell it to the private sector with a stronger broadcasting act in order to serve the people of Canada better.
I should like to turn for a few minutes to the bilingualism program which has been voted more than one billion dollars since the inception of the program. Has this program served the country well? Has it given us a sense of community from coast to coast? Has it produced a generation of young people coming out of our school system with a basic knowledge of a second language? The answers to these questions are obvious. It has not. When one reflects on what could have been done through the last decade with wise application of this resource in view of such an important national need, one can only cry with anguish.
Our Post Office will cost some $568 million in 1978 over and above revenues received. When we compare this to the $700 million cost for the postal system in the United States which serves ten times our population, again one has to question the competence of the management of the Canadian Post Office. Anarchy exists in our Post Office. Bad management and incompetence are facts of life which must be corrected.
In the last 15 years federal government spending has risen from $7 billion to $45 billion. In this period taxes have increased 239 per cent and personal incomes 142 per cent. I believe that we are very close to taxpayer resistance in Canada, and is it any wonder? During the last three years of restraint operating costs have risen 56 per cent, and total federal spending is up 45 per cent.
Last year the Unemployment Insurance Commission cost us $4.4 billion, and the 1979 main estimates show that the commission will need a further $5.3 billion next year.
In my opinion all of this is a negative weight on the taxpaying work force of the country. In 1978 the prediction for inflation, according to the Conference Board, is 7.4 per cent. According to the Bank of Montreal it is 8 per cent. The Bank of Canada says 7.8 per cent, yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) says 7 per cent. The present rate is 9 per cent, and even if the consumer price index did not increase at all between May and December of this year, we will still have a

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
rate of inflation well over that stated by the Minister of Finance. We are into an area of consumer price index increases as a result of our 90-cent dollar, and there are serious consequences for national consumer purchasing power. I would like to remind the House of that now famous quote, which is as follows:
I am confident we have got a grip on the problem and . .. will wrestle inflation to the ground. We are going to bring inflation under control-that I pledge to you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on May 27, 1974. Here is another famous quote:
You can never spend more than you have; otherwise you have endless inflation.
The Prime Minister was reported to have said that in the October 20, 1975 Maclean's magazine.
The fact is that the government is able to pay for only 80 per cent of what it is spending today and we are not told what value we are receiving for that spending. One has to be watchful of the true direction and destination of this ship of state with this present Prime Minister on the bridge. As a direct result of this waste, incompetence and inflation we have a national nightmare for some 933,000 Canadians who today cannot find work in a nation with unbelievable wealth in its resources and potential wealth in its people. No single factor has caused more anxiety nor brought more shame to this country than the figure of one million jobless last winter. We did not experience an unemployment rate below 8 per cent in the first five months of 1978, yet eleven years ago the jobless figure was 3.8 per cent. Today it is 8.6 per cent. We stand to lose all that this country once stood for. The glue will yield if we do not act responsibly.
Believe me, hon. members opposite are so close to the malaise that they cannot see the facts. Waste exists not just in the management of government but also out in the private sector. The waste in the private sector is caused by a taxation system which encourages waste and gives incentive to waste, and I think that this is one of the major challenges any federal government has ahead of it in bringing about a taxation system which will tax cost, not profit, which is the incentive which makes the system work.
Credit must go where credit is due. The present government is the most wasteful in Canadian history. It has established an unmatchable standard of incompetence which has led to today's higher inflation and record high unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: You don't believe that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: I certainly do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Our balance of payments is also an indication of the failure toward which we are headed. Last year we had a deficit of $4.2 billion in our balance of payments. Even though we had a surplus in raw material and farm products, we incurred a deficit of $7.5 billion mainly in the service sector and, I want to stress this, in interests and dividends on the $50 billion borrowed abroad. We also had a $1.6 billion deficit in tourism. We recorded an unbelievable deficit of $11 billion with respect to manufactured goods.
Mr. Speaker, the premier of Ontario recently estimated that by balancing our current payment account with respect to finished products, we could generate some 170,000 additional jobs. Our economy is really suffering from a chronic illness. Our productivity and our competitive position is faltering. Many of our industries are threatened, namely textiles, shipyards, auto parts, television sets and other electronic equipment. No other province suffers as much as Quebec where 24 per cent of the labour force works in the manufacturing sector. Even though these industries are protected by tariffs, the fact remains that 36,000 Quebeckers have been laid off last year in the soft sectors which are the textile, clothing, footwear and furniture industries. The government of Quebec did take certain steps to help these sectors and among other things it has abolished the sales tax on these products. Yet the federal government has naturally hampered its efforts by refusing to grant the government of Quebec a fiscal transfer which would have enabled it to be on the same footing as the other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, because of the different priorities in each region, it is inconceivable to try and impose uniform solutions throughout the country. These solutions come late, much too late unfortunately, from a government which has run out of imagination.
We are not concerned about prevention or cure and, if we are we do not prescribe the proper medication-unless it is the drugstores that do not fill the correct prescriptions.
We have just been given a document entitled "A Time for Action". When I consider the economic situation I think it is not only time for action but time for a fast action. Of course, we are offered several answers but they come really late. For instance, the project announced by DREE to invest in touristic developments in the Gaspe Peninsula and the Lower St. Lawrence comes after years and years of representations and supplications. The Gaspe Peninsula is undoubtedly tourism-oriented, but that is nothing new, Mr. Speaker, yet only today do we decide to develop that industry. And we need to develop it if we want to balance our payment deficit in that sector.
As I was born in the Gaspe Peninsula where I lived for many years, I know much about fishing. It is an important sector of the economy of my region and this is why, Mr. Speaker, I participate with interest in the fisheries committee. I even have the opportunity to make interventions in the House like my colleagues from Newfoundland and the Maritimes to
Government Waste
ask for improvements in maritime fisheries even if it does not always please my colleague for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) who would rather have me keep silent. But I am too much concerned by the development of eastern Quebec to keep silent. With the advent of the 200-mile limit, the government suddenly realized that there is a fishing industry in Canada. So much so that after the demise of the fisheries department we shall see the birth of a new one called the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. We had the opportunity to discuss the lack of foresight of the government in that sector during the presentation of an opposition motion by my colleague for South Shore (Mr. Crouse).
And what about the mining sector. There have been lay-offs at Falconbridge and Inco in Sudbury. And in Gaspe there has been the closure of Madeleine Mines in Ste. Anne des Monts and the slowing down of production in Murdochville. However, little if not nothing has been done to encourage our mining industry. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a small digression. A Liberal government had to be defeated and a PQ government elected before shelved projects like the salt mines in the Iles-de-la-Madeleine and limestone deposits in Madeleine and Port Daniel in Gaspe could be dusted off and revived.
To conclude, I suggest that we can no longer continue to ignore the weak sectors of our economy and the poorer regions. The Canadian problem is one of regional disparity. As long as we do not make any effort to develop our country more equally I am afraid that social pressures will increase and that our economic problems will only perpetrate the division process.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have been provided with an opportunity to participate in this debate. At the outset, I should like to indicate that I concur in the motion before the House accusing this government of being the most wasteful in Canadian history.
I	do not want to deal specifically with the projects which exemplify government wastefulness, as the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) has so aptly done. I want to deal specifically with the area of unemployment. The government has been wasteful in handling the economy, to such an extent that at the present time there are over 900,000 people unemployed in Canada. That is a waste and drain in human terms as well as in economic terms.
Recently the treasury of the province of Ontario indicated that one out of every three graduates from now until the 1980s can hope to obtain employment. That should not ease the minds of all hon. members.
We have heard a lot about the number of man-days lost due to strikes and lockouts. The figures for 1978 released by the Department of Labour show that 278,200 man-days were lost in the month of February. I agree that is a lot of lost man-days; but for every man-day lost due to industrial disputes, whether lockouts or strikes, there are 30.5 man-days lost

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
due to unemployment. I calculated for the month of February, with 278,200 man-days lost due to lockouts and strikes, and extrapolating the man-days lost because of unemployment, that 9,730,000 man-days were lost due to unemployment. That is lost productivity to the nation as a whole. The estimated yearly financial loss to Canada amounts to $12 billion in income and output, or about $520 for every Canadian, man, woman and child. Unemployment affects both the working people and the victims of unemployment.
Another piece of interesting information came from some calculations done by the Canadian Labour Congress. Since 1974 unemployment has cost every Canadian family $11,000. Last year alone unemployment insurance payouts amounted to over $4 billion. What was the productivity in respect of that $4 billion? There was no productivity at all. This government should be ashamed of itself for showing in its estimates that unemployment insurance payouts are $4 billion, with not one iota of productivity to show for that $4 billion. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, people can sit on their asses and collect unemployment insurance with not one stitch of productivity to show for it. It is a shameful record that this government stands in its place trying to defend this this afternoon. It is projected that unemployment insurance this fiscal year will exceed $5 billion. That is a shameful record.
I cannot understand for the life of me the kind of decisionmaking and unplanned approach of which this government is guilty. I recently attended a committee meeting studying the bill dealing with the Export Development Corporation. We found consistently that government agencies were prepared to finance unemployment in this country. They used taxpayers dollars to create competitive industries abroad, not necessarily in third world countries but in countries such as the United States, when in fact they will not spend that sort of money in Canada to modernize those aspects of the economy that need modernization in order that they can be productive and compete for the sale of our products abroad.
We had a perfect example of that in respect of the layoffs by Inco and Falconbridge in the Sudbury Basin. We urged this government that in place of allowing these workers to go on unemployment insurance it ought to stockpile nickel, because it is more important for the workers to be productive and the value would be in the nickel produced. We felt this was better than allowing the companies to put 2,000 or 3,000 workers on unemployment insurance, and certainly better than getting into the whole process of transporting workers from the Sudbury Basin to Alberta, or wherever, at more cost to the taxpayers. We suggested, not only for the welfare of the worker in terms of his productivity but also in terms of his standard of living, that it was much better for a worker to be productive, working and receiving a pay cheque than being unemployed and receiving an unemployment insurance cheque. This party has consistently urged that approach on the government.

The government must involve itself in creating full employment in this country. We cannot afford to carry on, as we are at present, without a policy of full employment. We require a commitment to full employment rather than a policy of riding on the backs of the workers with 8.6 per cent unemployment, amounting to over 900,000 people unemployed.
The warning came in September of 1977. This is not something new to this government; it received warning in 1977. The warning went out to all industrial nations of the world. It went out from the chief of the International Monetary Fund, managing director Johannes Witteveen. He said that a continuation of anti-inflation programs would keep unemployment at record levels and slow economic growth to recession levels. He went on to say that it was the international responsibility of nations to pursue markedly higher rates of economic expansion if we are to get out of our current economic slump.
The effects of the government's anti-inflation program on the economy have been quite spectacular. As a matter of fact, writing for the Toronto Globe and Mail an economist, Arthur Donner, estimated that in the period from 1974 to the end of 1976 the Canadian economy lost $25 billion in real growth and 600,000 man-years of employment. This was a result of the government's anti-inflation program. If restraint continues, by the end of 1978, he estimates, we will have lost $49 billion worth of production and 1.3 million man-years of employment, and all this for a marginal effect on the inflation rate.
That prediction is coming true. The latest statistics on our productivity were published in the Globe and Mail this morning in the business section. It was pointed out there that the Canadian manufacturing sector of the economy operated at 82.7 per cent of capacity .n the first quarter, down from 88.3 per cent in the fourth quarter, the lowest level since the 82.5 per cent in the 1975 fourth quarter.
Obviously mismanagement of the economy has resulted in the cutback of our productivity as a nation, and that cutback in productivity manifests itself in the 900,000 people unemployed at the present time. The government knows well, and its own statistics department has given the figures, that even being very generous there are about 45,000 available jobs at any given time and 900,000 persons looking for employment in this country.
Time and again we have seen this government look for scapegoats. We have seen ads by the Unemployment Insurance Commission moving the blame away from the government. This government never accepts responsibility for mismanagement of the economy. It finds a scapegoat and diverts the attention of the Canadian public. The UIC has spent in excess of $1 million for advertisements suggesting very surreptitiously that there are people on unemployment insurance who have their hands in our pockets. Following that, it spent another $100,000 or $200,000 on a survey intended to show, in effect, that its advertising program was satisfying a large sector of the Canadian public. If that in itself is not a waste of taxpayers' money, I do not know what is.
June 14, 1978

This government refuses to move or interfere directly in the economy in a way that would establish full employment as a policy for this nation. For example, I have mentioned the capacity at which the Canadian economy is operating; at the present time it is 82.7 per cent. What did we see in the third last budget? We saw the government stimulating the corporate sector to the tune of $1.1 billion. That was a stimulation directed toward expansion. That $1.1 billion has been paid out, but where are the employment opportunities? Why do we expand an operation that is not operating at full capacity? Where is the logic in that? It seems to me that what the government has to do is stimulate consumption, especially among low income Canadians in order that they can improve their standard of living, and that money should have been pent for that purpose. It seems to me that that would have stimulated the productive capacity of the nation.
That lack of productivity indicates that we are not building enough houses in the nation. It is fairly obvious that the government is not providing the services which are essential to a modern economy. For example, there is the case of transportation where the government should have spent money directly to create employment in the service sector.
There are needs in our communities across the country. There are parts of my riding which still have one well in the centre of the town, and everybody goes down with a bucket to get water for the day's usage. There are still those communities that have outhouses in my riding, and this is 1978. This is not a Third World country, it is Canada. Some 42 per cent of the urban housing in my riding is still substandard. The government is still not building the kind of accommodation that bespeaks an industrially developed nation.
There was a PCB spill by the CPR that leaked into the water table, and the community has been unable to afford a water system so that the residents could be assured that they would not be drinking the polluted water. There are some facilities and services which are needed, and there are municipalities which have set their priorities, but because of a lack of capital they are unable to move forward with those particular programs. All of those programs are labour intensive, but what does the government do? It spends hundreds of millions of dollars on one-shot approaches such as Canada Works and Young Canada Works. These programs are Fine so far as they go, but they do not get at the problem of unemployment in the nation.
The government has a responsibility to make sure that there is work for every Canadian who wants to work. It is their responsibility so to arrange the economy, so to manage the economy that it does produce the jobs. I consistently hear that the post-war baby boom has created this great surge of unemployment. Listening to the government, one would think that there is no registration of births, that suddenly all of these young people who are now coming into the work force suddenly appeared as though they were springing out of the ground, from dragon's teeth. The way the government talks, one would
Government Waste
assume that births are not registered in this country and that we are not able to project the number of young people who will be coming into the work force down the line and, therefore, so arrange the economy. This government does not plan. There is no economic planning by this government.
I mentioned the situation of the Export Development Corporation. Here we have the EDC lending large multinational corporations long-term loan money to develop their overseas operations in direct competition with the operations they have in Canada.
While they are trading off the jobs in the mining sector in the long term for short term, high technology jobs, we have the government funding DREE. What is DREE trying to do? DREE is trying to attract industry to go into areas like mine. It is obvious that one is nullifying the other. If an industry receives an order from Inco in Guatemala to build whatever it is they are going to build, then, obviously, they expand the plant in southern Ontario. They are not going to build a plant in northern Ontario to produce that stuff. So, in effect, you have the one nullifying the other. There is no cohesive or meshed plan with respect to how to go about creating employment and how the EDC and the DREE program relate to each other. What is the interface of those two programs?
These branches of government are completely in isolation. The president of the EDC rubs his grubby little hands and says, "We made $18 million last year, we are here to make a profit." That is not good enough for the people, for example, who work in the mining sector, the pulp and paper industry or in the steel industry. They see that, in effect, Canada through its Crown corporation, the Export Development Corporation, is putting them out of business and contributing to their unemployment.
It seems to me that the workers who come through my riding office are not in the least bit interested in the $155 unemployment insurance cheque they get every week. They are interested in a pay cheque because in a pay cheque there is human dignity. This way they can keep their families without having to depend on the state or on the bureaucracy which keeps growing and growing.
As a matter of fact, I do not know why the government thinks it has to use its departments to fight the unemployment situation alone. The unemployment insurance office in Sudbury had to hire 11 people last week to deal with the increase in unemployment insurance cases. I do not know where the sense is in that at all.
The workers who go through the unemployment office and who are now unemployed are mostly the young, because they are the first ones to go there. But they are more interested in having a job; they are not interested in the unemployment insurance program. Yet the government runs its advertising program to suggest, very surreptitiously, that anyone who is collecting unemployment insurance is somehow or other ripping off the system. Anyone who is unfortunate enough to be caught in the unemployment insurance fiasco somehow or other gets the feeling he is stealing from the government or stealing from those who are working. It is a very inhuman

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
system, and I repeat to the minister and the government that they must stop the waste and the high unemployment that we have in the country. The government has to involve itself directly through municipalities and public programs in creating employment in those periods in the economy when certain forces beyond our control affect unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate this afternoon I would like to refer to one or two of the points raised by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) wherein he refers to an article he was reading in today's edition of the Globe and Mail. I think he was using some of those extracts to indicate what he considers to be real problems in the Canadian economy, lack of activity in the private sector, inadequate government direction, et cetera.
I would like to draw to his attention-I am not sure that we were reading the same article, presumably not-a front page article in this same Globe and Mail wherein there was very positive indication of some very substantial progress that seems to have occurred in the Canadian economy in the first five months of this year. This article was referring to reports that jobs are being created at the present time at a historically rapid rate. It refers particularly to the first five months of 1978, primarily in the manufacturing, transportation, communication, retail and wholesale areas. There is reference to 180,000 jobs having been created in the Canadian economy in the period January 1 to May 31, 1978. That 180,000 job figure would give an annual rate, if it was to continue at the present pace, of some 434,000 jobs per year. If that rate is achieved for the balance of 1978, it would be the highest rate since 1973.
In fact, 180,000 jobs, Mr. Speaker, created in the first five months is equivalent to the total number of jobs created during all of 1977. If that is not progress, Mr. Speaker, if that is not some indication of the kind of leadership that is being shown by this government, the kind of things that are happening in the Canadian economy at the present time, then I am not sure what sort of positive signs the member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is seeking.
Mr. Speaker, I think these figures are interesting enough that I would like to mention a few more of them from the same paper that the member for Nickel Belt was quoting. There has been an increase in the labour force-the highest ever-in the same five-month period of 525,000 people, whereas the increase was 308,000 for all of 1977. This, of course, is where the problem comes in, Mr. Speaker. Our labour force continues to grow at a rate higher than the Canadian economy is able to absorb. Nevertheless, the record figures on both sides, I think, are important to state because it is some indication of the extreme degree of activity that is going on.
At the present time, 57.1 per cent of the population of Canada is employed, which is up from 56.5 per cent as of last

December; 71.8 per cent of all men are employed and 42.8 per cent of all women. These increases, Mr. Speaker-and again I emphasize this-came from the private sector. This refers back to the motion we have before us today, by the member for Capilano (Mr. Huntingdon) regarding what he claims is the incompetence of the government in its handling of expenditures, and, presumably, of the economy. Yet we are told that the employment ratios in this country today are at the highest point they have ever been, and this is occurring mainly in the private sector.
Noted economists have stated that there is indeed strength in the Canadian economy at the present time. As I said in a speech in this House recently, that kind of news is not the kind of news that the official opposition in this country wants to see. It is not the kind of news that the unofficial opposition, the NDP, wants to see. But it is positive news, Mr. Speaker. It is important to state over and over again that while there are problems in the Canadian economy, problems that are being addressed by this government, there exist also very significant indicators of strength, and I think it is important that those go on the record. In fact, one prestigious investment firm, Wood Gundy and Company, because of recent news on the economic front, Mr. Speaker, is already revising its forecasts of job creation for 1978.
Coming back to the motion, Mr. Speaker, I have worked with my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano, on public accounts committees over recent years and I think we have both been conscious of concerns that the Auditor General has brought before the public accounts committee. In some cases Crown corporations, agencies or even departments of government, have perhaps adopted too enthusiastically the kind of direction that emanated from the Glassco commission of many years ago that encouraged less central controls and more expenditure initiatives at the departmental level. That gave the government some problems and, Mr. Speaker, as over-all expenditure levels of the government have increased, these problems have obviously become of a more acute nature.
The important thing to note is that the President of the Treasury Board, (Mr. Andras) and the government have faced these problems and have done two very important things in the last two years. The position of Comptroller General of Canada has now been firmly established. The first incumbent is now on board as of April 1, and I think this development is something my colleague the hon. member for Capilano, myself and others on the public accounts committee and other members in this House welcome enthusiastically.
In addition, the government has appointed the Lambert commission to look into all aspects of government expenditures and financial control. When the member for Capilano refers to incompetence, surely that must indicate that in his mind the government is doing nothing about these kinds of things. I think the record clearly shows that some very concrete and positive steps have been taken on every issue that the Auditor General has placed before this House of Commons and before the public accounts committee. That, Mr. Speaker, in my mind, is the kind of responsiveness that the Canadian public
June 14, 1978

want to see in their federal government, and it is the kind of responsiveness that this government has indeed shown over and over again.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that when the member opposite formulated his motion he made it so encompassing that one could probably discuss everything from sour cherry production in Ontario to energy conservation, all within the context of government competence. I would like to refer to one or two of the points that perhaps are included in his indication of incompetence, such as growth in the public service.
There is, Mr. Speaker, an allegation of waste in this area, and there is an allegation of irresponsibility on the part of the government. Yet, the man-year growth in the public service and the program of performance measurement that is now under way is something with which I think all members in this House should become more familiar, particularly the member for Capilano who I know is intensely interested in what is happening with the public purse.
The administration committed itself to restricting growth in the public service at the same time as it announced its program of fiscal restraint. It should come as no surprise when I say that the program has met with the same kind of success as the fiscal program has achieved.
The main estimates that the President of the Treasury Board introduced in February marked the second consecutive year that growth in the public service was held to six-tenths of one per cent. 1 mention those figures, Mr. Speaker, as against the figures I quoted a little earlier, to show the dramatic increase that is occurring in the labour force in the number of people working in this country. In the public service, the federal public service, the growth has been held to six-tenths of one per cent, which is a little over half of one per cent.
To record such a marginal increase, Mr. Speaker, it means that 18 departments had their man-year allocation reduced and 18 were permitted no increase. Thirty-six departments and agencies, generally service-oriented agencies such as the RCMP, the Post Office and national defence, were allowed more man-years to cope with specific problems confronting them.
Whenever we talk about cutting back government expenditures or not increasing government expenditures where new services are needed, some very basic questions come up. For instance, I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) in the House this afternoon. He has to decide which new homes in which cities are to be denied mail service in order to cut man-years. Should certain areas of the RCMP be cut and should the military be held in check? These are questions the administration has to wrestle with in order to maintain this near zero expansion of the public service in a country which is growing and developing.
In the same year as we have held manpower growth down to six-tenths of one per cent, the labour force in Canada increased by 2.5 per cent in 1977-78 and is projected to grow by a very significant amount. As I indicated earlier, no increases have been permitted for the year in the number of
Government Waste
senior personnel man-years for four consecutive years. That is an area that has come under attack from hon. members opposite at different times.
If further evidence is needed to demonstrate the responsibility of government, let me turn to the administration of some programs. The government has acted to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of its operations through the measurement of program performance. There has been considerable progress in this area since the experimental projects of the early 1970s. Departments now are required to have adequate and reliable means for measuring all programs in place by 1980.
Since government operations do not have readily identifiable indicators, such as profit or return on investment-the simple indicator that the private sector always has-many different kinds of indicators have been developed in the federal system. They use example indicators that relate results achieved to resources used and to planned results. They describe the service aspects of performance and focus on production-type measures. All of these help managers develop systems to assist them in assessing how well their programs are running.
This approach to program management is operating so well that it is fast becoming a tool on which decisions can be based and is an integral part of the management process. The monitoring of this process enables departments to evaluate whether changes or improvements can be made in the method by which a program is delivered; whether programs have outlived their usefulness and can be eliminated; or, whether priorities have shifted, making it more or less important.
Members of this House were given a copy of a report on "Performance Measurement" last fall. In light of this motion I commend this report to the hon. member for Capilano and to his colleagues on that side of the House. It denies, in practical working environment evidence, the allegations that prompted this debate today.
I might just mention in closing that the kinds of things we are saying and the effectiveness of government cutbacks are being recognized in various publications and articles, and by such writers as Dian Cohen who is never hesitant in criticizing the government on those aspects of the management of the economy where she considers the government is doing a poor job. In a recent article in a leading business publication headed "Ottawa Trying", Dian Cohen did indeed make reference to the fact that this time the government seems to be really talking business in its efforts to maintain a control over spending. That is one example. There are others by leading writers of the day.
When the hon. member for Capilano recommends we rework the whole tax system, as he did, and move to taxes based on costs, he has to understand what it would do to companies which are starting out in business that have losses for a number of years. This is getting into a system where profits are no longer taxed but where expenditures are taxed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, every time we have one of these motions I listen to the parliamentary secretary and he gives the usual government pitch. That is what this government has done over the last ten years as far as I am concerned. Certainly we have real problems in this country. The most important thing I can say about this is that this government has created most of them. The government does not tell us anything like that.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) on placing this motion before the House, a motion which the parliamentary secretary did not read. The part I like in terms of the record is the advent of television. Before television this government was able to bamboozle and flim-flam the people. I say to the people there is no need to read the papers; just turn on the television set. The government's incompetence, indecision, bungling and ineptness, as well as the flim-flam that forms the whole history of this particular administration, and in particular its front bench, can be seen via television.
I notice that the President of the Treasury board (Mr. Andras) has a book on his table. He is probably going to blast away at poor Ed Murphy. Thank goodness we have him. He is president of CJOR Radio. He prepared a book entitled "A Legacy of Spending". If I was rich enough I would buy this book and send it to every voter in the country, because it gives a history of waste. I want to read a few statements from this book-

No wonder the government does not want anyone to read this book. Let me just read the foreword. I do not even know who wrote it. It is some chap by the name of Lindsay B. Semple. It reads:
There have been many instances throughout history where there emerged a ruling elite with enormous control over the material resources and products of their subjects. One of two things normally occurred-either they continued to grow until they impoverished the producers in the nation state and of course themselves, or they were thrown out by revolution.
In Canada there has emerged a monstrous bureaucracy and state spending mechanism. As this resume clearly demonstrates it has exploded in recent years. It is uncontrolled and uncontrollable. The implications for the future of this country and you are awesome.
Ed Murphy should be highly commended for documenting this national tragedy. Read this resume carefully, copy it, and pass it on to your neighbours. It could be the beginning of a new awareness and perhaps even a movement to halt the insidious disease that infects this great nation. Lindsay B. Semple, M.A. (Econ.)
I do not know who he is, but he is certainly telling it as it is. Let me read another quotation. This is why the Liberals do not want anybody to read "A Legacy of Spending." I know the President of the Treasury Board has a copy. Here is a quote that really focuses attention on where the problem is:
"There is only one place where inflation is made in Canada and that is Ottawa. The unions don't make inflation for a very simple reason; the unions do not own a printing press on which they can turn out those multi-coloured pieces of paper called money. The reason you have inflation is because the government has been printing too much and spending too much." Milton Friedman, Nobel Prize Laureate in Economics, CBC Radio, Feb. 20, 1977.
Let me read another quote. This is the way the government operates. I quote from page 5:
As the spending becomes larger and larger every year, less and less disclosure exists.
I do not want to single out the President of the Treasury Board. Sometimes I wonder why all the cover-up. Why not tell the people the truth? We had a little get together here in terms of over-classification. If it had not been for the opposition, the Canadian people would not know there are a number of public servants over-classified because of this government's ineptness. As a result, we are losing some $19 million per year. That is only as a result of a study in the Ottawa-Hull area. Would we ever have known about that? No. We have to get these things flushed out somehow. Thank goodness there are people prepared to put their jobs on the line and pass a little brown envelope under somebody's door so that we know what is going on and can tell the Canadian people the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
The record breaking feats of this government are nerve shattering and unbelievable. I want to put something on the
Government Waste
record in terms of incompetency. I look at the smiling face of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Martin). There is another dead issue. They have not done anything. They did not start to think about the small businessman until we pushed them into it.
What about the 89 cent dollar? Did you ever see such indecision, not knowing what to do, until now we have a dollar which has been totally destroyed? This has led to a position where our imports have been adversely affected as well as confidence in this country. That is part of this government's record in terms of a "great feat."
What about government spending? Ten years ago it was $10 billion. Today it is $50 billion. Talk about restraint! What is going on in this country? Why the flim-flam? Why the dishonesty? By feeding inflation we have a deficit of $11 billion. We spend more than we take in. That is another part of this government's great record.
What about the one million unemployed? That is another great record for this government, breaking the one million mark in terms of unemployment. That is something which will go down in history.
Talking about records, what about this government's tremendous record in fragmenting the country? As a result of Bill C-56, some will get cheques and others will get deductions or tax cuts. It is blackmailing the provinces. Has anyone here ever seen the likes of it?
What about the all-time record of selfishness? Make the worker take 6 per cent in terms of a pay increase while this government sits idly by and watches inflation reach 9 per cent. The yearly total will be about 11 per cent. In October, 1978 this government said it would be 4 per cent. What kind of dishonesty are we experiencing here?
What about another all-time record in deceit? If we attack or question this government in terms of its policies vis-a-vis the province of Quebec, what do they call us? We are either a separatist or we are helping the separatist cause. In other words, this government believes it is God, that you dare not attack it; you are wrong if you do and you are helping the separatist cause. What a lot of nonsense. I wish I could swear like the Prime Minister!

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, after reading the motion before us and listening to the comments made so far I can only say I am appalled by the extravagance, the bias, the naivete and the lack of balance in both the motion itself and in the remarks of most of the hon. members who have taken part in this debate.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander)-my good friend on a personal basis-has been in his usual good voice. Two or three years ago I was tempted to describe his comments as bombast and rhetoric. We have had a double dose today in a speech which contained very little substance, very little by way of constructive suggestions.
The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) told us that when he came here from the business world he got the impression that this institution was an "Alice in Wonderland" creation. The hon. member for Hamilton West made a similar comment. After listening to the observations of members opposite I have to say they are living in a dream world. They have no sense of proportion.
Of course Canada is experiencing economic problems. Of course there are ways by which the efficiency of government
Government Waste
can be improved, as is the case in every country. But their performance would be more credible if only occasionally they would acknowledge that we do not live upon an isolated island totally detached from the rest of the world. We do not. We are a leading trading nation; one in four of our jobs depends on our ability to export. But those exports are influenced by economic conditions throughout the world and we cannot escape that fact. Hon. members opposite would have far more credibility if they admitted, just on occasion, that there were other factors affecting our economy. Because if they ever became really responsible, instead of being merely critical-a state of affairs which I personally believe would be disastrous-they would have to take these things into account.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) talked, for instance, about the Export Development Corporation. He talked about the export of jobs. Mr. Speaker, that corporation exists in order to assist Canadians to produce goods and sell them abroad. The goods being sold are Canadian goods and it is Canadian jobs which are associated with their production. Does the hon. member suggest we can stand idly back from the kind of competition which goes on around the world and let other people handle these opportunities? I can assure him it would be somebody else's goods which would be sold and other people whose jobs would be involved. He should recognize that the corporation is serving a good purpose and performing a good function.
I wish to concentrate in my speech today on more specific points relating to my responsibility in the portfolio I hold and into the allegations of waste made so bluntly and extravagantly in the motion. Where have members opposite been in the last several months? Where were they when I introduced the main estimates which showed that for the third consecutive year a restraint program unparalleled in recent history had been undertaken?
Where were they when a few days later I placed in the hands of every member, whether they read it or not, a document called "The Impact of Administrative Restraint" which talked about a saving of $100 million annually by administrative action alone?
Where is there recognition that the office of Comptroller General has been created? Where is there recognition that the Auditor General Act has been passed and that it enhances his powers and gives him powers which I think are second to none for that kind of parliamentary officer anywhere in the world? I say again that I am appalled, in the light of that record, that hon. members opposite would bring forward such an ill-conceived and irresponsible motion as the one which is being debated today. It is ill-conceived and irresponsible because it lacks substance. I have to say that it is long on politics but devoid of substance.
Let me review the record of this government since we announced our restraint program. Hon. members will recall that we announced that the growth of spending over time would not be permitted to exceed the growth in the gross national product. We tried to balance that comment. That
80045-39%

June 14, 1978
