comment was a candid acknowledgement that expenditures had been rising too quickly in the past under all governments in this country and, frankly, nearly all the governments of the western world.
It was a candid acknowledgement that something had to be done, that government spending could not go on rising at the rate it had been and that it had to be checked or else the economic well-being of the country would be jeopardized. Never before had a Canadian government made such a commitment in advance to such a policy, and while the commitment was dramatic, I can tell the House now that it is my view that the results have been even more dramatic. We have been setting targets consistently which have been below gross national product growth forecasts. We have been holding spending below those targets.
I will not claim that it has been easy. Some important proposals have had to go down the drain. Some very ambitious projects had to be scaled down from their first presentations. In the first year I recall that more than $1 billion had to be trimmed from departmental forecasts shortly before the estimates were tabled.
Without going into all the details I hope the House will allow me to delve briefly into the past and to highlight the spending estimates for this year. In 1976-77, which was the first full fiscal year under the restraint program, we held spending to more than $1 billion below our target. That gave us a 10.2 per cent increase over the previous year, while the current dollar g.n.p. for that same period grew by about 13.4 per cent.
The 1977-78 fiscal year, which just ended March 31, was even tougher. When main estimates were tabled a year ago, I announced that total spending would be $45,120 billion. It was subsequently reduced. First, we reduced the publicly stated target by $670 million to make room for the tax cuts announced in the March, 1977 budget.
Following that we faced some unforeseen and rather extraordinary requirements for economic spending and for transfer payments to the provinces. For example, we decided we needed another $200 million for various job creation programs. We had to find another $440 million for cash payments to the provinces because the income tax points we transferred to them the previous fall under the agreement covering hospital insurance, medicare and post-secondary education did not produce as much revenue as had been expected. So we had to find another $440 million and stay within these reduced ceilings.
We did, despite those pressures, keep the lid on, and I was really quite pleased to be able to inform the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), in the preparation of his April 10 budget, that we now expected total spending for fiscal year 1977-78 to be at least $200 million below the final target we had set; in other words, about $44,250 billion. That was a full $870 million less that the target set when I tabled the main estimates in February of 1977.

Coming to fiscal year 1978-79, in February I tabled the main estimates, as hon. members will recall. They included a statement of a maximum total spending target of $48.8 billion, which was an increase of about 9.8 per cent over the 1977-78 expenditure forecast, which was then $44.45 billion. So for the third consecutive year we are well within the forecast growth of the gross national product.
That was the figure I tabled in February, but here again history is repeating itself. In conversation with the Minister of Finance in trying to make as much room as possible in terms of the deficit for the tax cuts he announced on April 10, we further reduced our spending plans by another $350 million. So the 1978-79 growth pattern will be within about 9.5 per cent over the previous year, not the 9.8 per cent predicted in the main estimates.
I think the figures speak for themselves. In 1974-75, the mid-seventies, that responsive and expensive period of minority government, spending increased 28.3 per cent over the previous year. In 1975-76 it dropped to 18.4 per cent. It went down to 10.2 per cent in 1976-77 and, taking into account the one-time only changes in our budgetary system, to about 10 per cent in 1977-78, and we have a forecast percentage increase this year of 9.5 per cent.
I do not think that is a litany of incompentence and wastefulness. What that sounds like to me is a record of financial management which is responsible and responsive because we have slowed down the rate of government spending. We have brought it into line with the growth of the economy, and we are trying to do that without going in the other direction and undermining the economic development and requirements of this nation.
1 was interested in a comment by the C.D. Howe Research institute in its "Policy Review and Outlook" for 1978, published by that responsible and respected organization. Judith Maxwell said that it was evident that the country had made a good deal of progress in eliminating the excesses which were so alarming on previous occasions, particularly back in the 1972, 1973, 1974 period.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: Was that a Liberal government then?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: She was referring to all governments of all political stripes in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext: It was a Liberal government, though, was it?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Yes, with Conservative governments in Ontario and some other places, unfortunately, and governments of other flavours in other provinces of this country.
Judith Maxwell also said that on fiscal policy governments have moved a long way toward controlling the rate of growth in their spending, and that restraint has occurred at all levels of government. However, I want to put a balance into this. She wrote also-and I agree, in spite of the fact that my own inclination would be to want to see our expenditures going down even more rapidly than they are-that it is also important to keep in mind that constraints on government spending,
June 14, 1978

as necessary as they may be in the long run, act as a constraint on economic recovery and, given the balance of the economy in 1977, governments must try to find a balance between their desires to get their finances in order and their responsibility to stabilize economic activity.
While members of the official opposition particularly want to decry the rate of reduction in government spending and boast about $2 billion tax cuts and that sort of thing, the fact is that ours is a responsible approach to ratcheting down and getting our spending in better order; but perhaps it does not have the dramatic and assumed political appeal of the Draconian measures I have heard suggested. Those suggested measures have never been backed up by indications as to how those changes will be accomplished. In any event, the rate of growth in government spending has been slowed down.
Perhaps the telling argument to that effect was the show put on by honorable members opposite during consideration of the main estimates in February. At that time, the spokesman for the official opposition accused me of being and continuing to be a spendthrift. He indicated that no progress has been made. Yet the spokesman for the New Democratic Party took the opposite view and suggested that we were being far too niggardly and should continue to increase our spending.
I have a rather comforting feeling that perhaps we are on the right course. If either one had agreed, I am afraid I would have been somewhat nervous, returned to the drawing board and rechecked my thinking. I do not want to argue political philosophy in this debate. I am attempting to assemble some of the facts in order to demonstrate, in my view, the questionable value of the motion before us.
I have put the following question before the House during similar debates in consideration of main estimates and budget debates in the past: What really prevents us from making greater inroads in the growth of government spending? I have indicated that I would like to see the growth rate drop even faster than it has so far, with one caution or proviso which I illustrated by quoting the C. D. Howe Research Institute.
One of the major reasons, of course, is the statutory obligations and commitments approved by the House to share in the financing of provincial activities and many, many other programs mainly of a social nature. The increases in such programs are unquestionably built in and difficult to control. Approximately 60 per cent of the budgetary estimates for 1978-79 fall into this category.
Reductions in these statutory programs, or even cuts in their rates of growth, are made much more difficult by the fact that the majority of them involve transfers to individuals or to other levels of government. I am referring to old age security payments, fiscal transfers to the provinces, family allowances, the Canada Assistance Plan, unemployment insurance, postsecondary education, medicare and extended health care.
These few programs to which I have referred account for approximately 40 per cent of the budgetary estimates for this year. When one adds to the statutory 60 per cent of estimates
Government Waste
requirements for other contractual programs or formula payments, such as those for CMHC housing programs where we have agreements with the provinces, occupational and manpower training, fiscal transfers to the territories, veterans' pensions and allowances, and many more, there is obviously not much room left to cut back on government spending without very deep and sober thought.
To put it another way, approximately $10 billion of the $48.8 billion target for 1978-79 will be transferred to the provinces. Another $10 billion plus will go to individual Canadians. These payments supplement the incomes of millions of Canadians-senior citizens, growing families, workers temporarily unemployed, people undergoing new training, native people and veterans. In an economic fashion, these payments are used largely for shelter, food, clothing and other basic necessities.
Major reallocations of resources have been taking place constantly in order to accommodate increases in statutory programs. They have been taking place during every fiscal year without our limit on total spending being exceeded. While the final accounts are not available for 1977-78, I am confident spending will be held to approximately $44,250 million, which is $870 million below the ceiling I announced before that fiscal year began. That was accomplished in the face of some very large, unforeseeable demands of almost $1 billion for programs such as job creation and payments to the provinces. Without the increases in the payments to individuals and to the provinces, many of which programs are indexed, our rate of increase in spending would have been less than 3 per cent this year.
I would have liked to have the time to deal with some of the other comments made during the course of this debate, particularly those which apply to my portfolio. I enhance the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Martin) and his references to the control on public service man-year growth. I would have liked to elaborate more on the administrative restraint program which is ongoing. Not only does that program save over $100 million a year now, but it is reducing-

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I should like to correct something which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) said. He said, when the estimates came down last March, that I accused him of being a spendthrift. I should like to correct that statement. I do not think he is a spendthrift. I am convinced his government is a spendthrift. I accused him of peddling flim-flam in terms of explaining government spending patterns. If one requires any other evidence of flim-flam on the part of this minister, he only has to read his speech of today. Again his speech was full of inexcusable flim-flam.
The minister is President of the Treasury Board. That organization has three areas of responsibility. One is to manage government spending-the estimates-examine the

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
budgets of various departments, approve such budgets, estimate government spending annually, and supervise government departments to ensure that they are effective and efficient. The second is the responsibility for the public service. The third is the management of the public service bilingual program.
Dealing with the first responsibility, let us look at how well it has been fulfilled by the Treasury Board. Turning to the 1976 report of the Auditor General on managing government spending, the Auditor General said the following:
I am deeply concerned that parliament-and indeed the government-has lost or is close to losing, effective control of the public purse.
In terms of that aspect of its mandate, the Auditor General, who is not a party hack for the Progressive Conservative or New Democratic parties, but is an officer of parliament, said that the Treasury Board had failed in that regard. How does the Treasury Board look after the public service? Through the proverbial brown envelope route and as a result of an audit, we have found out that approximately 16 per cent of public service positions are misclassified. That means of any seven public servants performing the same task, six are classified properly and the seventh is classified too high. In other words, the seventh is being paid more than the other six for doing the same job.
Is this going to build up the morale of those six doing the same job as the seventh but getting paid less? Is it going to soothe the Canadian public which has to pay more than it ought for the services of that seventh individual? If you use that example to measure the success of Treasury Board in fulfilling its responsibilities in terms of the public service, it has failed miserably.
Surely no one in this country has the gall to claim the bilingual program has been administered properly when examples of abuse, misuse and mismanagement in that program are too legion to enumerate. In all three areas of responsibility the Treasury Board has failed miserably.
The present minister has not been in that position for long and cannot be expected to carry the entire blame. Those who preceded him are now in even higher positions of authority. We can understand why the Treasury Board has been so poorly run when we look at the records of the previous ministers. For example, a previous minister of the Treasury Board is now Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). When we consider what he is doing with his responsibilities in that area we can clearly understand why the Treasury Board is in such poor shape.
The minister opened his remarks today by saying it is time we faced up to the facts. He said that we do not live on an island, and admitted we had some problems. It was very gracious of him today to admit that we have problems. I guess his admission that he is trying to do something about cutting back on spending is an admission of the accuracy of the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). If he did not tacitly agree that there was tremendous waste and incompetence in the way things were being
[Mr. Andre.)
handled, he would not be engaged in this program about which he has been bragging. In this way he has as much as admitted failure in terms of the incompetency of that program.
The minister indicated we are on the right path now. He said that this government is on the path toward fiscal responsibility. He said the government is going to bring spending under control. He mentioned some figures which I will get to in a minute, because they were really nothing more than flimflam.
Not long ago, on April 13, 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said on national television that we would be on the way to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control, that spending vast sums on welfare, education and other programs while allowing inflation to continue would merely place hundreds of thousands of Canadians on a treadmill they could not escape.
The Prime Minister then dedicated himself to fiscal responsibility and to bringing government spending under control. That was in 1969. Since then spending has increased by 240 per cent. Why in the world would any sound Canadian believe this minister today when he says things will be different as a result of some new program? We had the clear example of the Prime Minister dedicating himself on national television to restraint, and we all know what happened as a result of that dedication. The fact of the matter is that no one should trust what that Prime Minister or that government has to say. There is an old expression that when a con man catches you once, that is his fault; but if he catches you twice, it is your own fault. I do not think the people of Canada will be fooled twice by this less than honest government.
The minister is proud of the fact that he has controlled expenditures by keeping growth to less than 10 per cent. I believe he referred to 9.8 per cent, or possibly even 9.5 per cent, and he was patting himself on the back. How did he do that? The implication was that he accomplished this by being very frugal and by cutting out waste and the misappropriate spending of money.
The fact of the matter is that the way he did this was by disguising spending. Until the estimates were placed before us last year, Crown corporation loans formed part of government spending. They recognized that when the EDC made a loan as an agent of Her Majesty it was exactly the same as the government making a loan, and it was included in the estimates. All loans by EDC or any other Crown corporation, such as CMHC, were included. Such loans are excluded from the estimates this year.
When you take from the estimates $1 billion in Crown corporation loans, it looks as though government spending is $1 billion less. If that is not flim-flam, what is it? I suggest it is pure, unadulterated flim-flam, and certainly it is being less than honest with the Canadian people.
The minister had the gall to stand in the House and pat himself on the back, so much so that his arm must be sore claiming he has been effective in cutting back. But what he really has done is to disguise and hide spending from the
June 14, 1978

people of Canada. That really is intolerable and I do not think the people of Canada will be fooled by it.
That is not the only way large expenditures were disguised. This government pushed $1 billion in spending on the provinces which had formerly been shown in the estimates. Again that makes it look as though the government has reduced the level of expenditure by $1 billion. By subtracting loan payments from expenditures you engage in flim-flam. All you are doing is disguising the spending which actually occurs.
Let me give another classic example of this procedure. Whenever a Crown corporation runs up a tremendous debt, this government turns it into equity. All of a sudden the debt disappears, as do the interest payments associated with the debt. All of a sudden by magic the Canadian public no longer has the obligation to pay the interest on the debt, because the debt through transfer has been turned into equity. That is a marvellous scheme, but it is nothing more than flim-flam. This is the type of thing that medicine show snake oil salesmen use, and the public will not fall for it again.
The other thing I want to take the minister to task for is his statement that the government has appointed a Comptroller General with unlimited powers to police government spending. His words were unfounded because the Comptroller General has in fact no such powers. He occupies the position of a deputy minister and no more. We hope and pray his efforts will be effective; do not get us wrong in terms of motivation. However, the claim that, through creation of the position of another deputy minister, the government will cure all the problems is simply inaccurate.
It would take more than 20 minutes, more than 40 minutes, more than a week and more than a month, to list and describe just a few of the examples of waste and extravagance on the part of this government. Let me talk about one additional example in view of the presence in the House today of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne).
I am prompted to speak of this example because of a memo that came over my desk a couple of weeks back in which the Postmaster General had the colossal gall to say that Canadians could post a letter more cheaply than the citizens of any other country in the world. He had the colossal gall to propose that complete fabrication, and it is a complete fabrication. He completely and conveniently dismissed the fact that the Post Office is operating with a deficit this year of S571 million.

The Postmaster General completely neglected to include in this calculation the Post Office deficit of $571 million this year. Of course we pay for this deficit. The fact of the matter is that in a family of four, that expenditure amounts to the mailing of 700 letters a year. In other words, we are being charged for
Government Waste
700 letters a year that we do not mail to cover the deficit of the Post Office, that superbly run organization.
The Post Office in the last decade, the Liberal decade under this present administration, has increased the amount of mail it carries by 18 per cent. It has gone from some five billion to six billion pieces of mail each year. In that same time postal employees have increased by 43 per cent, from 46,000 to 66,000. In other words, every employee in the Post Office now handles 60 per cent of the mail that he handled ten years ago. This is what automation has brought us, that great new introduction of this government. That automation has, in fact reduced the productivity of every postal worker by 40 per cent, plus it has given us collectively a bill of $571 million to cover its losses.
I wish to cite one other example at this point, and that is with regard to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. I mention it because of this hassle with Petro-Canada, and because I had to go back and look at the debates on Petro-Canada. The then minister of energy, mines and resources, Donald Macdonald, stood up in the House and said that Petro-Canada will be a marvel and will bring in all kinds of energy, and that Crown corporations in energy do very well.
Well, Mr. Speaker, Atomic Energy of Canada is an outstanding example of how effective a Crown corporation can be in improving Canada's energy situation. It was just two or three months later that the people of Canada found out that Atomic Energy had lost something like $300 million in Argentina, that we had given untold millions to Shaul Eisenberg and who knows how much to Korea and Japan. We found out that that organization could build reactors and give them away. They have cost Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars, and there is plenty of evidence that in fact some of that money may not only have been wasted but used in a corrupt manner. As I indicated, I could go on and on, but thanks to Mr. Ed Murphy a lot more people know about the waste of this government.
It is important to realize the consequences of all this waste upon this country, and this is something that we as responsible parliamentarians have to be concerned about. An example is "Proposition 13" in California which was voted on by the taxpayers a couple of weeks ago. That could not happen here because we do not have as democratic a system, but there was a message there. Anybody in this House who deludes himself or herself into thinking that Canadians do not share some of the same views as those California taxpayers is not being of service to this country or their constituents. The fact is there is a growing resentment in this country toward taxes and taxation, not just in terms of the level, but because of how much the public see wasted and how much incompetence they see.
I had an accountant tell me the other day that he has clients asking him to do things in terms of claiming tax deductions for which, if he had suggested them ten years ago, they would have fired him. He gave this by way of an example. Ten years ago there was a willingness on the part of people to pay taxes. They felt obliged to pay as responsible citizens, that they were

June 14, 1978
Government Waste
fortunate to be part of this country and to be able to pay their share. They certainly did not resist it. Although I do not think anybody voluntarily pays, they did not resist or resent it. This is not true today, for there is great resentment and concern about the misspending of the government.
Another thing that happens, and which is equally important, is a general discrediting of government and parliament. There is a feeling among the public that the government cannot be trusted. The public feel that they have been lied to too often in the past. The result of this is that we as parliamentarians get painted by the same brush. There is a cynicism with regard to parliament and government. There is the feeling of them and us, an adversary mood of parliament versus the people. It is not government of the people for the people. We are going back to the old days of when the state was a tyrant and the people were its subjects, and that feeling is increasing in this country.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a very serious situation because if it is not arrested and turned around we will have a much less democratic country than you and I, and I am sure anybody in this House, plan for. Cutting that waste is important in terms of the funds and dollars involved, but I think it is even more important in terms of the confidence of the people. When governments waste, spill and misuse public funds, they bring upon themselves the discredit of the people and as a result weaken our society and the democratic fabric of our nation.
I know there are others who wish to speak. I could go on for hours on this subject, but I will sit down and allow some time for the remaining speakers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas H. Lefebvre (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT WASTE AND INCOMPETENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems obvious from reading that motion and listening to hon. members of the official opposition that nobody on the other side of this House took the trouble of reading the last report of the Auditor General of Canada. For their information I feel I have to bring to their attention what everyone has known for several months. On page 9 of his report of March 31, 1977, the Auditor General writes:
Other positive, constructive and important actions by the government since the tabling of my 1976 report, some of which will be referred to in subsequent paragraphs of this part and all of which have significant impact on financial control, include:
the announcement on December 16, 1976, by the President of the Treasury Board of new government policy and guidelines concerning the commercial practices of Crown corporations;
the enactment by Parliament of the new Auditor General Act and its proclamation by the Governor General effective August 1, 1977; the granting by Parliament on the advice of the government of a significant increase in resources to the Audit Office through main estimates for 1976-77; and
the release on August 18, 1977, by the President of Privy Council of a paper setting out Government Proposals on the Control, Direction and Accountability of Crown Corporations.

Still on page 9, paragraph 2.10 says, and I quote:
Taken together, these actions by the government and Parliament comprise, in the phraseology I used in my 1976 report, "strong, appropriate and effective measures" to achieve ultimately a satisfactory system of financial management and control within the federal government and the restoration to Parliament of an appropriate degree of control over the public purse.
Those are the words, Mr. Speaker, of a very competent person, namely the Auditor General of Canada.
I should like to come back now to some of the claims made by the opposition. Where do they want to start in achieving these greater economies? Will they start with payments to individuals which went up by $926 million this year, or with payments to pensioners, the unemployed, young families, or will they attack all three groups? I forgot the veterans, which is a small group. Perhaps they want to start their savings there.
If this hits too close to their constituents, maybe they would like to take on the provinces since 46 per cent of the increase in our spending this year resulted from increased transfer payments. Before they do that I should remind them that equalization payments for 1978-79 alone account for 26 per cent of the total revenue for Newfoundland, 29 per cent for Prince Edward Island, 27 per cent for Nova Scotia, 24 per cent for New Brunswick, 10 per cent for Quebec, 13 per cent for Manitoba and slightly more than 2 per cent for Saskatchewan. That is one of the questions that has not been answered today.
In his speech the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) pointed out that this government made further advances in the reduction of waste and the improvement of control. One of the most obvious measures that the opposition does not mention very often is the legislation which created the position of Comptroller General. When the appointment was made the Auditor General said that he was more than pleased, and in reply to questions in the public accounts committee on several occasions he indicated his approval. No one on the other side has mentioned that.
Aside from the legislative changes there is also progress in the field of financial administration, some of which I would now like to detail. On November 8, 1977, Treasury Board issued a circular to revise the policy on grants and contributions. Principal features included revised definitions of a "grant" and a "contribution" and clarification of the requirements for Treasury Board approval of terms and conditions for all payments of contributions.
A significant change, restricting advance payments to three months, will prevent long-term financing of projects at an interest cost to the federal government. It will discourage the payment of contributions without progress reports and without an accounting for the amount claimed by the recipient.
All departments and agencies are reviewing their grants and contribution programs against the new policy, and where they do not meet the requirements will seek approval of revised terms and conditions from the Treasury Board.
June 14, 1978

The financial administration branch has also completed a review of cash control procedures in departments and agencies resulting in a new policy directive. The directive provided for proper physical security of cash, an adequate division of duties, periodic verification of advances, and the manner in which funds will be transferred from one responsible officer to another. All departments and agencies were required to report on the manner in which this policy was implemented.
A policy directive has also been issued to govern the use of departmental credit cards. The general policy is that credit cards will not be issued to employees. Recognizing that certain departments have a need for such cards, they may be issued on the written authorization of the deputy head who is not permitted to delegate this authority. Conditions of use and payment must be agreed to by the employee. Monitoring of credit cards accounts takes place monthly by a departmental financial officer.
At present the financial administration branch is doing a study of practices and alternatives for the deposit and transfer of public money. The study includes various methods in use by other organizations in Canada and abroad. The objective of the project is to develop a policy, and a method for the deposit and transfer of public money which will reduce the amount of money in transit at any point in time and improve internal control over funds deposited and transferred. A major revision to the guide on financial administration issued in 1973 is also under way.
We are also developing a policy on interdepartmental charging to classify the types of interdepartmental services provided, various methods of charging for such services and the conditions to be considered in deciding whether or not these methods should be applied.
To ensure accuracy and timeliness of financial reports, the branch is completing the development of a policy and related system to ensure that payables at the end of a fiscal year are
Government Waste
reported in the accounts of Canada. This policy will give effect to the implementation of recommendation 24 of the report on the study of the accounts of Canada.
The branch is also preparing a draft of a concise guide to the estimates and public accounts, which was requested by the Standing Committee on Public accounts.
Another group within the financial policy development division is responsible for the development of policy and standards for financial systems employed by departments and the approval of departmental systems proposals to ensure that they meet established policy and standards. Work of the group includes completion of a study to determine the most appropriate methods of achieving timely and accurate financial reports for government departments and agencies. A policy on departmental financial reporting systems and related standards has been drafted, and several studies are currently being done on specific proposals for improving the departmental financial reporting system of the Department of Supply and Services.
For several years the Public Service Commission has been offering an accelerated series of courses in professional accounting and other related subjects necessary for accreditation by one of the professional accounting bodies.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would just say that this motion provided an opportunity for the President of the Treasury Board, the parliamentary secretary and myself to reply to these unfounded charges made by the opposition.
